blurb: Every repo and skill from the 17 November issue that I could source, with what each does and the setup steps from its own README.
intro: Issue #50 had six repos and one AI skill, and this page covers five repos and the skill. If you edit video with a coding agent, start with ffmpeg-skill: one `npx` command and it works offline. If you are worried about spyware on your phone, Zero Breach Toolkit has a browser check that needs no install.

items.name: ffmpeg-skill
items.cost: Free and open source (MIT), no API keys or account
items.works_with: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI and any MCP client
items.short: Gives your coding agent 42 local FFmpeg tools to cut, caption, reframe and export video, then check the result.
items.what: ffmpeg-skill is an agent skill that teaches your agent a fixed routine: probe the file, edit it, then check and verify the output. It ships 42 tools that run `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe` on your machine for cuts, joins, silence removal, captions, overlays, loudness, platform exports and more. Every tool can also be called as an MCP tool.
items.who: People who edit video with a coding agent and want the work to stay on their own machine. If you only need a one-off trim, plain FFmpeg will do.
needs: FFmpeg 6.1 or newer with the components it needs (on a Mac the README says to use `ffmpeg-full`)
Node 16 or newer, only for the `npx` installer
Optional: a local speech engine such as faster-whisper, only for captions from speech

steps.title: Install FFmpeg
steps.text: This is the Ubuntu and Debian command. On a Mac the README uses `brew install ffmpeg-full`, and on Windows `winget install Gyan.FFmpeg`.

steps.title: Install the skill
steps.text: This installs it for Claude Code. Add `--cursor`, `--codex` or `--all` for other agents.

steps.title: Or install it as a Claude Code plugin

steps.title: Or run it as an MCP server
steps.text: For clients that have no shell.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Take `interview.mp4`, keep 0:45-3:10 and 5:00-6:30, and make it exactly 60 seconds for Reels.

watch: The tools write files. With the `overwrite` option they replace an existing file, so keep a copy of your original footage.
A plain Homebrew `ffmpeg` on a Mac lacks some filters, so a few tools will not run until you install `ffmpeg-full`.
The optional speech engines download their model weights the first time they run. The audio itself stays on your machine.
Installed copies do not update by themselves. Run `npx ffmpeg-skill` again to refresh.

items.name: Claude-BugHunter
items.cost: Free and open source (MIT for code, CC BY 4.0 for content)
items.works_with: Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex CLI, Hermes Agent and Google AntiGravity
items.short: A bundle of 83 skills and 15 slash commands for authorized bug bounty and external red-team work.
items.what: Claude-BugHunter is a skill bundle for bug hunting and external red-team engagements. It holds 83 skills drawn from 681 disclosed reports, covering web bug classes, recon, enterprise platform attack chains, and report writing. The skills load by topic when you describe what you are testing, and a 7-question gate checks scope before anything is submitted.
items.who: Security researchers on bug bounty programs and pentesters with a signed engagement. It covers the internet-facing attack surface only, so internal Active Directory, C2 and post-exploitation work are out of scope. If you do not have permission to test a target, this is not for you.
needs: Claude Code for the plugin route, or another supported agent for the copy install
Written permission to test the target: an in-scope bug bounty asset, a pentest engagement letter, a CTF or your own systems
Optional: Burp Suite with its MCP server extension

items.name: PaperOrchestra
items.cost: Not stated in the README. You pay for the AI model and API calls you use.
items.short: A Google Research pipeline of AI agents that turns your ideas and experiment logs into a LaTeX research paper draft.
items.what: PaperOrchestra is a multi-agent framework from Google Cloud AI Research for writing AI research papers. Separate agents handle the outline, literature review, section writing, refinement and plots. It takes your ideas and experiment logs and produces a LaTeX manuscript in a conference template.
items.who: Researchers who are comfortable with Python and Conda and want to test automated paper drafting. The README says it is not an officially supported Google product, so treat it as research code.
needs: An API key for the model you use: Gemini (or a Vertex AI project) or OpenAI
A Semantic Scholar API key, for the literature search
A folder with your raw materials and a LaTeX template folder

steps.title: Install the dependencies
steps.text: Run this in the cloned repo.

steps.title: Add your keys
steps.text: Create a `.env` file in the project root with the keys for the models you use, such as `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY` and `SEMANTIC_SCHOLAR_API_KEY`.

steps.title: Run the pipeline
steps.text: Point it at your raw materials, a LaTeX template such as `templates/cvpr2025` and an output folder. Add `--use_plotting true` to have it make figures.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Run `python paper_writing_cli.py` with `--raw_materials_dir`, `--latex_template_dir`, `--output_dir` and `--use_plotting true` set to your own folders.

watch: Your keys live in a plain `.env` file. Keep it out of version control.
The optional demo can email results to you, which needs your email address and password in `.env`. Skip it if you would rather not store those.
The dataset used in the paper is not in the repo yet. The README says it will be released later.
Every run calls paid model APIs, so watch your usage.

items.name: Zero Breach Toolkit
items.works_with: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android collections and iPhone backups
items.short: A free offline check for traces of known mercenary spyware such as Pegasus and Predator on computers and phones.
items.what: Zero Breach Toolkit looks for published traces of known mercenary spyware on Windows, Mac and Linux computers, Android collections and iPhone backups. It also checks links, emails, files and QR codes, and points out settings left open on your devices. It reads only, makes no network requests during a scan, and says in every report what it could not check.
items.who: Anyone worried about spyware, especially journalists, activists and people who help them. If you think you are being targeted right now, the README says to contact the Access Now Digital Security Helpline or Amnesty's Security Lab first.
needs: For the Python version: Python 3.8 or newer, no extra packages and no admin rights
For an iPhone: a local backup on your computer
On a Mac: Full Disk Access for Terminal or the app, so it can read Safari

steps.title: Phone backup? Use the browser check
steps.text: Open archivegenocide.com/scan/phone on the computer that holds the backup and choose the backup folder. Nothing is installed and nothing is uploaded.

steps.title: Get the toolkit for a computer
steps.text: There is also a double-click app on the latest release page. The README notes the Python version avoids antivirus warnings because you run the source directly.

steps.title: Download the latest indicator lists
steps.text: Run this from the toolkit folder. It is the only step that uses the internet. Use `python3` on Mac and Linux.

steps.title: Close your browsers and chat apps, then scan
steps.text: A menu opens. Press Enter for the standard check.

steps.title: Check a phone collection or backup
steps.text: Put the folder path in quotes.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Run `python -X utf8 scan/zero-breach-toolkit.py --quick` for a faster first pass, then read the "What could not be checked" part of the report.

watch: A clean result is not proof you are safe. It only finds spyware someone has already published traces of.

The project is anonymous and the downloadable programs are not code-signed yet, so Windows and macOS will warn you. Running the Python version from source avoids that, and the README shows how to verify a download.
Reports can hold usernames, file paths, browsing details and message excerpts. Keep them out of shared or synced folders.
`--update` contacts the internet to fetch indicator lists and check for a newer version. Scans themselves stay offline.

items.name: Git for Global Law
items.cost: Free (CC0). The law text in each country's repo is under that repo's own terms.
items.works_with: Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Codex and any MCP client
items.short: The world's law as git history, so you can see any provision as it stood on any date and which law wrote each line.
items.what: Global Law puts each country's, state's or court's law in its own git repository, where every commit is one law taking effect. This repo gathers them as submodules and ships Python tools to show a provision on a date, list its changes, diff two dates and blame each line. It also has an MCP server and a free hosted connector.
items.who: Lawyers, researchers and developers who need to know what a law said on a given day. If you just want to look something up, the hosted search on the project's site needs no install.

steps.text: A shallow clone keeps it small.

steps.text: This adds the US Code. Swap in any other path from `manifest.json`.

steps.title: Read a provision on a date
Use it from your coding agent
steps.text: Opening the clone in Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code or Codex starts a local MCP server with the same tools. Hosted chat apps can use the free connector at `https://global-law.lexifina.com/mcp`.

try.label: From the README
try.text: Run `python3 tools/law.py log united-states/federal/usc/title-11/1182.md` to see every change to that section and the law that made it.

watch: Opening the clone in a coding agent starts a local MCP server on its own.
Coverage differs by country. Some publishers keep only today's text, and `manifest.json` says which.
Court decisions are added separately and the tools leave them out unless you name them.

items.name: audit-channel-risk
items.cost: Needs a TubeLab plan (the MCP is included from Starter). Searches cost credits; reads are free.
items.works_with: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI and other agents that read SKILL.md
items.short: Scores how likely a YouTube channel is to be demonetized or terminated, with the proof and what to fix first.
items.what: This skill checks one or more YouTube channels against YouTube's channel monetization policies, which it reads fresh on every run. It compares the channel's videos with similar channels that were terminated or lost AdSense. You get one HTML page with a demonetization score, a termination score, the evidence behind each and up to four actions to reduce the risk.
items.who: YouTube creators and studios who want an early warning on monetization risk. You need a TubeLab account, so if you do not plan to pay for one, skip it.
needs: A TubeLab account on the Starter plan or above
The TubeLab MCP connected in your agent
For Cursor and other IDE agents: a TubeLab API key, which needs the Pro plan

steps.title: Install the skills
steps.text: This installs the whole YouTube research set, including this skill.

steps.title: Or install the Claude Code plugin
steps.text: This also connects the TubeLab MCP.

steps.title: Connect the TubeLab MCP
steps.text: Skip this if you used the plugin. The first call opens a TubeLab login.
steps.code: claude mcp add --transport http tubelab https://public-api.tubelab.net/mcp

try.label: A first prompt
try.text: Audit youtube.com/@handle for demonetization and termination risk.

watch: Searches spend TubeLab credits. Channel, video, transcript and comment reads are free.
The skill gives TubeLab access through your account login (OAuth) or an API key.
A low score means no warning signs were found. The skill itself says it does not mean the channel is safe.
It writes an HTML report file to your machine.
